claim: The MIND-Set database includes mentally healthy participants and patients with diverse, highly prevalent non-psychotic psychiatric disorders (i.e. mood disorders, anxiety disorders, addiction, ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity).
source: This database provides us with a sample of mentally healthy participants and patients with diverse, highly prevalent non-psychotic psychiatric disorders (i.e. mood disorders, anxiety disorders, addiction, ASD, ADHD, and their comorbidity).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the composition of the MIND-Set database sample.

claim: Linked ICA performs multiple, simultaneous ICA factorizations that share the same unique mixing matrix.
source: Linked ICA performs multiple, simultaneous ICA factorizations that share the same unique mixing matrix and has been shown to be a powerful tool for identifying independent components (ICs) that reflect patterns of shared variance across multiple neuroimaging modalities (Groves et al., 2012, Groves et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Groves et al., 2012 and 2011 to support the description of linked ICA methodology.

claim: Linked ICA has been shown to be a powerful tool for identifying independent components that reflect patterns of shared variance across multiple neuroimaging modalities.
source: Linked ICA performs multiple, simultaneous ICA factorizations that share the same unique mixing matrix and has been shown to be a powerful tool for identifying independent components (ICs) that reflect patterns of shared variance across multiple neuroimaging modalities (Groves et al., 2012, Groves et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Groves et al., 2012 and 2011 to support this claim about linked ICA's capabilities.

claim: Linked ICA has established relationships of interindividual differences in multimodal brain components with behavioral measures and clinical profiles in autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
source: Linked ICA has already established relationships of interindividual differences in multimodal brain components with behavioral measures and clinical profiles in specific patient groups, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and Huntington's disease (Garcia-Gorro et al., 2019; Itahashi et al., 2015; Wolfers et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites Garcia-Gorro et al., 2019; Itahashi et al., 2015; Wolfers et al., 2017 to support this claim.

claim: Linked ICA has established relationships of interindividual differences in multimodal brain components with behavioral measures and clinical profiles in attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

evidence: The manuscript cites Garcia-Gorro et al., 2019; Itahashi et al., 2015; Wolfers et al., 2017 to support this claim.

claim: Linked ICA has established relationships of interindividual differences in multimodal brain components with behavioral measures and clinical profiles in Huntington's disease.

evidence: The manuscript cites Garcia-Gorro et al., 2019; Itahashi et al., 2015; Wolfers et al., 2017 to support this claim.

claim: Linked ICA has not yet been used to investigate core mechanisms of psychopathology transdiagnostically.
source: While linked ICA has provided a more coherent insight into the neural mechanisms within these specific populations, it has not yet been used to investigate core mechanisms of psychopathology transdiagnostically.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this gap in the literature.

claim: The same disturbances in structural and functional brain networks may be associated with core symptom domains that transcend traditional disorder categories.
source: It is important to adopt a transdiagnostic approach since the same disturbances in structural and functional brain networks may be associated with core symptom domains that transcend traditional disorder categories (Menon, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Menon, 2011 to support this claim.

claim: Psychopathology can best be understood on a continuum from health to mental illness.
source: Since psychopathology can best be understood on a continuum from health to mental illness, we also included mentally healthy participants, which allows us to study the brain and biobehavioral dimensions of interest along a wider range from health to psychopathology (Kotov et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2022; van Oort et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kotov et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2022; van Oort et al., 2022 to support this claim.

claim: High levels of comorbidity suggest shared underlying mechanisms across diverse non-psychotic psychiatric disorders.
source: We investigated the diverse non-psychotic psychiatric disorders (i.e. mood disorders, anxiety disorders, addiction, ASD, and ADHD) together as high levels of comorbidity suggest shared underlying mechanisms (van Eijndhoven et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites van Eijndhoven et al., 2021 to support this claim.

claim: Symptoms across various major domains cut across the diagnostic boundaries of mood disorders, anxiety disorders, addiction, ASD, and ADHD, with transdiagnostic symptom dimensions related to the negative valence domain.
source: In addition, numerous studies that investigated these disorders separately provide converging evidence that symptoms across various major domains cut across the diagnostic boundaries of these disorders, with, among others, transdiagnostic symptom dimensions related to the negative valence domain (e.g. repetitive negative thinking) and cognitive systems domain (e.g. regarding cognitive control problems) (Kerns et al., 2015; Koob and Schulkin, 2019; McTeague et al., 2016; Richey et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2014; van Eijndhoven et al., 2021; Woody and Gibb, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies (Kerns et al., 2015; Koob and Schulkin, 2019; McTeague et al., 2016; Richey et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2014; van Eijndhoven et al., 2021; Woody and Gibb, 2015) to support this claim.

claim: Symptoms across various major domains cut across the diagnostic boundaries of mood disorders, anxiety disorders, addiction, ASD, and ADHD, with transdiagnostic symptom dimensions related to the cognitive systems domain.
source: In addition, numerous studies that investigated these disorders separately provide converging evidence that symptoms across various major domains cut across the diagnostic boundaries of these disorders, with, among others, transdiagnostic symptom dimensions related to the negative valence domain (e.g. repetitive negative thinking) and cognitive systems domain (e.g. regarding cognitive control problems) (Kerns et al., 2015; Koob and Schulkin, 2019; McTeague et al., 2016; Richey et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2014; van Eijndhoven et al., 2021; Woody and Gibb, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies (Kerns et al., 2015; Koob and Schulkin, 2019; McTeague et al., 2016; Richey et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2014; van Eijndhoven et al., 2021; Woody and Gibb, 2015) to support this claim.

claim: Disturbances in the same brain networks may underlie core symptom dimensions across diverse disorders.
source: Interestingly, disturbances in the same brain networks may underlie these core symptom dimensions across these diverse disorders (McTeague et al., 2016; Menon, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites McTeague et al., 2016 and Menon, 2011 to support this claim.

claim: Vulnerability to stress is a common feature across a broad range of psychiatric disorders.
source: It is clinically well established that vulnerability to stress is a common feature across a broad range of psychiatric disorders (Ingram and Luxton, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ingram and Luxton, 2005 to support this claim.

claim: Mood and anxiety disorders are characterized by a maladaptive stress response as their central feature.
source: Mood and anxiety disorders are characterized by a maladaptive stress response as their central feature (de Kloet et al., 2005; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites de Kloet et al., 2005 and Sharma et al., 2016 to support this claim.

claim: Vulnerability to stress plays a key role in addiction disorders, with impaired coping with stress being implicated in the onset, maintenance, and relapse in these disorders.
source: Vulnerability to stress also plays a key role in addiction disorders, with impaired coping with stress being implicated in the onset, maintenance, and relapse in these disorders (Koob, 2003; Koob and Schulkin, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Koob, 2003 and Koob and Schulkin, 2019 to support this claim.

claim: Neurodevelopmental disorders show clear indications for increased stress sensitivity, as exemplified by arousal and emotion regulation problems.
source: While neurodevelopmental disorders have a relatively stable, trait-like course, there are clear indications for increased stress sensitivity, as exemplified by arousal and emotion regulation problems, which in turn may lead to the development of negative valence symptoms and stress-related comorbidity (Kerns et al., 2015; Richey et al., 2015; Rommelse et al., 2011; Shaw et al., 2014; van Eijndhoven et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kerns et al., 2015; Richey et al., 2015; Rommelse et al., 2011; Shaw et al., 2014; van Eijndhoven et al., 2021 to support this claim.

claim: The experimentally controlled stressor induced mild psychological stress, with an increase in subjective stress.
source: The analyses confirmed that our experimentally well-controlled stressor induced mild psychological stress, with an increase in both subjective stress (median subjective stress score after neutral movie: 3, after aversive movie: 5; T = –12.50, p<0.001) and heart rate (median heart rate during neutral movie [beats per minute]: 65.59, during aversive movie: 67.10; T = –8.60, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of subjective stress scores showing a significant increase.
